analysis.one_liner: Lets state attorneys general enforce state consumer protection laws against airlines.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote after being referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal aviation law generally preempts state rules over airline prices, routes, and service, which courts and regulators have read to shield airlines from most state consumer protection enforcement. This bill would add a provision saying that federal preemption does not stop a state attorney general from enforcing state laws against unfair or deceptive business practices and unfair methods of competition when it comes to air travel and its advertising and sale.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers, who would gain a new avenue of recourse when airlines engage in deceptive advertising or unfair practices, since state attorneys general could pursue such cases under state consumer protection law.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends federal aviation law to state that nothing in the federal preemption provisions over airline prices, routes, and service prevents a state attorney general or other duly authorized state or local official from enforcing state laws prohibiting unfair or deceptive business practices or unfair methods of competition with respect to air transportation or its advertisement and sale. [S2] [S3]
It defines 'State attorney general' as the chief legal officer of a State and covers states, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Airlines and air transportation sellers, who would lose the protection of federal preemption from state consumer protection and competition law enforcement, and could face state lawsuits over advertising and business practices; some compliance costs could be passed into ticket prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill could expose airlines to inconsistent consumer protection standards across many states, since each state's laws and attorneys general could enforce different rules on the same national airfare advertising and sales practices. This is the fair objection to opening a federally regulated interstate industry to state-by-state enforcement. [S2]

Because the bill only restores state enforcement authority and does not itself create new consumer rights or remedies, its practical benefit depends entirely on individual state attorneys general choosing to bring cases. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give airline consumers a meaningful avenue of redress through state consumer protection laws, at the cost of exposing airlines to potentially patchwork state enforcement of a national industry. The stakes are real but modest: it clarifies enforcement authority rather than mandating new standards, and its value depends on state officials acting on it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late September 2000 and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, where it sat until the 106th Congress ended three and a half months later without a hearing, markup, or vote. [S1] [S5]

narrative.text: Representative Tom Tancredo introduced the bill on September 22, 2000, joined by Representatives Schaffer and Udall of Colorado. [S1] [S3]
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure. [S5]
No further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines are better off, because federal preemption continued to shield air transportation from state consumer protection and competition law enforcement. Travelers gained nothing from a bill that never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Tom Tancredo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to clarify that state attorneys general can enforce state consumer protection laws against airlines.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 22, 2000 and took no further action before the Congress ended, so the bill never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny: a Republican sponsor with one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor, all from Colorado; no votes were ever taken, so the partisan split on the substance is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would have ended airlines' practical immunity from state consumer protection and unfair-competition enforcement under federal preemption, exposing them to state attorney general lawsuits over advertising and business practices. Its failure left that shield in place; travelers bore the cost of limited recourse against deceptive airfare practices.
